web_evidence.title: Recess
web_evidence.note: A contemporary New York Review of Books structural review says Kaufman tells the story through exchanges of letters and memoranda plus intact student notes and notebooks, corroborating participant-authored documentary narration rather than an external third-person narrator.

web_evidence.title: Up the Down Staircase by Bel Kaufman
web_evidence.note: A detailed full-book review explicitly identifies Sylvia as the first-person narrator in her long letters and teacher-to-teacher memos, while noting that other documents and the dialogue-only first and last chapters lie outside her narration.

search_log: Searched "Up the Down Staircase" Bel Kaufman with narrator, first person, point of view, epistolary, excerpt, letters, diary, frame narrative, and narrative technique terms.

Opened the Penguin Random House authorized excerpt and book description; the excerpt covers only the dialogue-only opening, while the description characterizes the whole-book correspondence structure.

Opened Google Books editions and contents; publisher metadata described the novel-wide assemblage of memos, letters, directives, notes, and papers, but the preview did not expose sustained interior prose through the web reader.
Opened the 1966 New York Review of Books review, which analyzes the complete novel's construction from letters, memoranda, student notes, and notebooks.
Opened a detailed 2025 full-book review that explicitly calls Sylvia the first-person narrator through her letters and memos and distinguishes the remaining documentary material.

Searched scholarly repositories and PDFs for structural analysis; an LSU dissertation landing page was accessible but its full text returned 403, and other academic PDFs could not be opened reliably, so they were not used as evidence.

Ran targeted exact-phrase searches for ambiguous Goodreads quotations, including the Payroll Division passage, the isolated postscript, the turkey-wishbone line, and Sylvia's teaching-work complaint; only the last yielded useful surrounding book context.
person_note: The novel is a polyphonic epistolary/documentary narrative rather than a conventional continuous narrator's account. Sylvia's letters and intraschool notes provide the controlling story line in participating first person, while signed student writings add other first-person documentary voices; under the methodology, multiple first-person narrators remain FIRST. Administrative slips and memos are constitutive but often grammatically unmarked, and the opening/closing dialogue and local quoted speech do not create a second- or third-person base. Quotes labeled dialogue upstream that explicitly say 'I am writing' were therefore used as constitutive epistolary evidence without changing their buckets. The only residual uncertainty concerns a few clipped quotations whose document boundaries are missing, not the whole-book person.
